messages.subject: Re: Changes in sampling intervals
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adam,

Is this a recent version of the package, updated from Github via remotes::install_github("ctmm-initiative/ctmm") ?
If so, would you mind sending me a minimal working example (data + script) that can reproduce the error so that I can fix it?

With fast=TRUE, a discrete time grid is constructed to approximate the sampling schedule. If dt isn't small enough, then the grid doesn't well approximate the true sampling schedule and different times can get bunched together.

In your script:
You're turning the location error on for model fitting, but I don't see any calibration data nor prior being used. This is generally unsafe, unless the data already have error estimates (such as Argos data).
You're overwriting the fitted error estimate with TRUE... I'm not sure what this is intended to do.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Highly Irregular Sample Rate
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ronena,

That looks fair for home-range and resource-selection estimation. If there isn't too much data, you might try variogram() with CI="Gauss" to calculate better confidence interval estimates and see if the increase in semi-variance from 0.5 km^2 at 2 weeks lag to 1.5 km^2 at 4 months lag is significant. You might also consider if the data need to be segmented further. Maybe the hawk moved nests or something?

An asymptote on the variogram is required for home-range estimation and resource-selection in general, regardless of what package you are using, and whether or not the package can check the stationary assumption.

dt.plot() shows all of the sampling intervals in order of size. So it looks like your most common interval is 1 minute (but some are much less) and 1 hour does not appear to be a very common interval, though intervals greater than 1 hour are very infrequent, so maybe the tag is trying to get at least a fix every hour.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Varigram Interpretation help
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kristy,

More parameters in the summary() don't indicate that the model is better. You don't want extraneous model features that are not supported by the data. The variograms all look pretty similar to me. Since you have so few data points, you might consider fast=FALSE,CI="Gauss" in variogram(), but I don't think it will make much difference. This already looks pretty clean.

For your area estimates, if you have units=FALSE in summary() then the output will be in SI units, which you can then convert to square kilometers with the %#% operator.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: overlap with small sample size/short durations
messages.subject_clean: overlap with small sample size/short durations
messages.body_plain:
Hi Danny,

ZcTag044 does appear to be stable for about 20 day, and if the theoretical variogram of the fitted model runs through that trend, then that would be a success. Tags 6-18 are harder to judge, but could also be compared to fitted models. Tag 3 appears too brief to judge, but I don't see any residency so far.

In my mind the classical analysis would be to report an average home-range size (from resident data) and how often individuals disperse (corresponding to segmentation) and an estimate of dispersal ranges (from non-resident data). In a more nomadic species, you can't necessarily make those distinctions, as the individuals are continually dispersing, and there I would just report the large nomadic ranges.

It may be necessary to model the location error, if it is comparable to the distances traveled between the sampled locations. There is a vignette('error') for this: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/error.html

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Changes in sampling intervals
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adam,

fast=FALSE,PC='direct' is numerically exact, but its too slow with very large datasets. fast=TRUE with a preconditioner is for improved computational speed on larger datasets. If the distributions look very similar, then you can feel safer rolling out the faster algorithm on your entire dataset, if you need that speedup. But with recent versions of the package, the default fast=NULL will do a pretty good job at choosing good arguments for your dataset.

eobs location accuracy columns should be detected and imported into the telemetry HDOP column, with the point estimate of the location error set to 1 meter. You want to put a prior on that, as detailed in the vignette('error'): https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctmm/vignettes/error.html
Then you would want to turn error on in the guess, but not modify that after fitting.

For the coati dataset, this would look like the following:

data(coati)
UERE <- uere(coati) # copy over error structure
UERE$UERE # here there is only one location class 'gps' - your data may differ
UERE$UERE[,'horizontal'] <- 1.4
UERE$DOF[,'horizontal'] <- 2.5
summary(UERE,level=0.5)[,,'horizontal'] # most e-obs are between 1 and 1.6
uere(coati) <- UERE # calibration data would be preferred

GUESS <- ctmm.guess(coati[[2]],CTMM=ctmm(error=TRUE),interactive=FALSE)
FIT <- ctmm.select(coati[[2]],GUESS,trace=3)

summary(FIT)

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Varigram Interpretation help
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kristy,

You need to take the DEM and derive a pixel surface area raster, which you can get from the slopes and pixel areas. Then with the AKDE projected coverage areas, you can calculate the 3D surface area within the desired coverage probability (e.g., 50% and 95%).

I haven't coded 3D speed estimation into ctmm yet. But if you extract the slopes over an individual's path, then you can approximate 3D speed from the trigonometry as

Speed.3D = Speed.2D * E[1/cos(slope)]

with the expectation value of 1/cosine(slope). The big assumption in this calculation is that speed doesn't substantially change with slope.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Changes in sampling intervals
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adam,

All of the default algorithms in ctmm are O(n) or O(n log(n)), meaning that computation time scales linearly or almost linearly with the amount of data. Analyzing the individual with 42k locations should only take 10 times longer than analyzing an individual with 4k locations. So, assuming everything is working right, being patient should work.

ctmm.select() with trace=3 should give you a per-model progress bar that fills up as the optimization completes, so you can see that progress is being made.

Many functions have a 'cores' argument if you are running on UNIX (Linux or Mac) that can be used to parallelize aspects of the computation, though it is almost always better to parallelize at the top level in your loop over individuals. Both ctmm.select() and optimizer() have a cores argument. If you are analyzing one individual on UNIX then control=list(cores=-1) could speed up the optimization considerably on a large dataset, as your 42k-point likelihood function then gets evaluated multiple times in parallel. (On a small datasets, the optimizer will fork too frequently, and your operating system will terminate the process.)

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Varigram Interpretation help
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kristy,

Judging from the plots, it looks like your AKDE has anisotropic covariance and kernels and your "KDE" has isotropic covariance and kernels. This is another variable that can impact home-range estimation, in addition to autocorrelation. Also, in your original list of fitted models, the 6th model is isotropic OUf and not IID. So I suspect this is comparing anisotropic OUf AKDE to isotropic OUf AKDE.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: HRE guess returning infinite
messages.body_plain:
Hi Johanne,

I haven't coded a home-range table function, but there is such a function for the model fits in ctmmweb. You should just be able to run sapply() over summary()$CI with units=FALSE.

There is RSF functionality in ctmm that doesn't require the specification of an available area, but, instead, estimates the available area and propagates that uncertainty (and also adjusts for the autocorrelation): https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/RSF.fit.html
But it looks like AMT wants object formats that you can export to from ctmm: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/export.html

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Minimum sample size
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a small dataset of Argos locations for 3 individuals over two summers. I have filtered out low-quality points. I have an average of 18 observations per individual, ranging from 4 to 43. My question is, do my samples have enough points to trust the HREs?

Thank you,
Vlad
messages.body_snippet:
Hello,

I have a small dataset of Argos locations for 3 individuals over two summers. I have filtered out low-quality points. I have an average of 18 observations per individual, ranging from 4 to 43.

messages.subject: Re: Minimum sample size
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vlad,

If you turn on the location error model, then you shouldn't have any problems keeping the lower quality location estimates: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctmm/vignettes/error.html

4 good quality location estimates is enough for home-range estimation, if they are not sampled too closely in time and if there is enough variance in the movement compared to the location error. You will find this out quickly when selecting an autocorrelation model and you get back the effective sample size for the area estimates, DOF[area] .

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Lorenzo,

With the data that you sent me, the summary() of the tracking data shows:

$`longitude range` [1] 13.21300 13.29266
$`latitude range` [1] 46.34345 46.39001

but the summary of the TIF file shows:

extent : 13.02221, 13.07831, 46.1996, 46.2497 (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)

so the extents of the tracking data and raster do not overlap. The raster is south-west of the tracking data. You have to zoom way out to see both. By default, the ctmm::plot() function focuses on the data, but you can set the extent as you want.

Also, if you want to do RSFs, then you will want to use an extent of spatial data much larger than the extent of the tracking data, so that the available area can be properly fit.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: AKDE vs MKDE
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris (or anyone that has knowledge on this subject),

I have a non-code-diagnostic question.

I recently came across the Benhamou (2011) paper on the MKDE and Biased Random Bridges (BRB). On the surface, it appeared that this method was appropriately accounting for autocorrelation by modelling the movement process with realistic options (unlike Brownian motion).  However, the results of the MKDE appear to be closer to the occurrence distribution rather than the range distribution. Is this true? And therefore, the MKDE does not attempt to extrapolate beyond the observed data, and therefore generally underestimates the home range (corresponding to the range distribution) with autocorrelated data? If so, was the occurrence distribution its intended purpose? Or is there a conflation problem going on here?

Thanks for any insight.

Best,
Odd

messages.subject: Re: Changes in sampling intervals
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adam,

The base models in ctmm are stationary and this is a non-stationary behavior, I would segment the data into 2-3 spatial clusters and then calculate 2-3 corresponding range estimates.

If you want, you can then aggregate those individual estimates in two different ways (with different biological interpretations) using mean(...,sample=FALSE), and/or pkde():
mean() to give the mean range distribution, under the assumption that these are the only areas (and you can weight by time utilized).
pkde() to give the mean range distribution, under the assumption that these are a representative sample of areas (and you can weight by time utilized).

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: AKDE vs MKDE
messages.body_plain:
Hi Odd,

Yes, MKDE is an occurrence distribution, where the movement model used is a BRB, and the end result will tend to be smaller than a range estimate. Also, because some variance in the data is being modeled as drift (rather than diffusion) it should end up smaller than a regular Brownian bridge, as well.

MKDE was introduced before the range/occurrence distinction was noticed, so I'm not sure if this was the intended purpose, but an occurrence distribution would be the best use case for MKDE, regardless.

Best,
Chris

>
> I have a non-code-diagnostic question.
>
> I recently came across the Benhamou (2011) paper on the MKDE and Biased Random Bridges (BRB). On the surface, it appeared that this method was appropriately accounting for autocorrelation by modelling the movement process with realistic options (unlike Brownian motion).  However, the results of the MKDE appear to be closer to the occurrence distribution rather than the range distribution. Is this true? And therefore, the MKDE does not attempt to extrapolate beyond the observed data, and therefore generally underestimates the home range (corresponding to the range distribution) with autocorrelated data? If so, was the occurrence distribution its intended purpose? Or is there a conflation problem going on here?
>
> Thanks for any insight.
>
> Best,
> Odd

messages.body_plain:
Hi Adam,

robust=TRUE will not help when there is no signature of velocity autocorrelation in the data, but only when the sampling distribution is heavy tailed, and velocity autocorrelation cannot be detected in part of the sampling distribution.

If in your better 15-minute data, tau[velocity] is well under 3 hours (8 times per day), then there's nothing you can really do. But if you are on the margin, then you can make sure you are using all of your data as best you can - not discarding high HDOP locations and using a good location-error model.

Alternative to speed estimation, you can also estimate diffusion rates if you can resolve a position autocorrelation parameter (tau[position]).

Best,
Chris

Ok, great - And what would the definition of diffusion rates be in this context? What exactly is the difference between daily diffusion and calculating the daily distance using velocity?

Would this code from a previous post still be relevant in extracting the diffusion rates?

# FIT must be BM or IOU: CTMM=ctmm(range=FALSE) in ctmm.guess
diffusion <- function(FIT,level=0.95,units=TRUE)
{
  FIT$range <- TRUE
  DIFF <- ctmm:::area.covm(FIT$sigma)
  DOF <- 2*ctmm:::DOF.area(FIT)
  DIFF <- ctmm:::chisq.ci <http://chisq.ci/>(DIFF,DOF=DOF,level=level)
  if(units) { DIFF <- "km^2" %#% DIFF %#% "day" } # otherwise SI units of m^2/s
  return(DIFF)
}

Thanks,
Adam

Hi Jason,

You just need to take the quote marks "" off of FALSE. TRUE and FALSE (or T and F) are boolean values in R, whereas quote marks enclose character/string values.

As for getting all plots into kilometers, you could leave the units argument alone and expand the plotting limits to be at least a kilometer across, then the units will automatically switch over. It wouldn't be hard for me to add an option to fix the units, though. I will add that to the to-do list.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I've been used the pkde function to estimate population ranges for different species of seabirds and am also hoping to be able to calculate the overlap of these ranges. Charlotte

messages.body_plain:
Hi Charlotte,

Chris walked me through this process a couple months ago and I'm happy to share! I had to overlap several PKDEs of different elk subpopulations and then also had to overlap elk subpopulation PKDEs with individual wolf AKDEs. Below is the code I used:

### overlapping elk subpopulation PKDEs ###

## combine lists of elk subpopulation PKDEs into one list
## so here you have to convert each PKDE (in my case, 5 different PKDEs) into a list and then combine them into a single list
winter20_elkGroups <- c(list(ldN=ldN_winter20_PKDE), list(ldS=ldS_winter20_PKDE), list(sdN=sdN_winter20_PKDE), list(sdS=sdS_winter20_PKDE), list(res=res_winter20_PKDE))

## then you can use the overlap() function on that compiled list
winter20_elkGroups_overlaps <- overlap(winter20_elkGroups)

## change array to df and then export as csv (I needed my overlap percentages as a csv - so here's the code for that too)
winter20_elkGroups_overlaps_df <- data.frame(winter20_elkGroups_overlaps$CI)
write.csv(winter20_elkGroups_overlaps_df, "\\winter20_elkGroups_overlaps.csv")

And here's the code I used to overlap PKDEs with an AKDE:

### overlapping elk subpopulation PKDE and individual wolf AKDE ###

## combining list of wolf AKDEs with elk group PKDE
ldN_winter2019_elkWolf <- c(ldN_2019_winter_wolves_AKDEs, list(Elk=ldN_winter19_elk_PKDE))

## calculating overlap
ldN_winter2019_elkWolf_overlaps <- overlap(ldN_winter2019_elkWolf)

## change array to df and then export as csv
ldN_winter2019_elkWolf_overlaps_df <- data.frame(ldN_winter2019_elkWolf_overlaps$CI)
write.csv(ldN_winter2019_elkWolf_overlaps_df,"\\ldN_winter2019_elkWolf_overlaps.csv")

Let me know if you have more questions!
Avery

messages.subject_clean: Coordinate Inconsistencies Between Dataframe and Telemetry Object
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jason,

as.telemetry() looks for long,lat and, failing to find that, UTM coordinates for import, but it does not retain the UTM projection, because UTM zones are not assumed to be constant within nor across datasets.

By default, as.telemetry() chooses a safe projection (2-point equidistant), which you can read off with projection().

You can set the projection to UTM using projection()<- assignment: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/projection.html

UTM is also fine if the animal is staying within the UTM zone.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: HRE guess returning infinite
messages.body_plain:
Hi Johanne,

If Z[red]² increased, then the goodness-of-fit became worse. But I'm confused about what you are doing. Error model fitting and selection is for calibration data (not tracking data), and supplying a prior is for when you don't have calibration data.

Informative prior parameters should give credible intervals that approximate the unknown prediction intervals of the population. So, in this case, GPS devices usually have a location error that ranges from a few meters to 10-20 meters at HDOP=1, and your credible intervals should reflect that. There are a number of GPS devices tested in https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.06.12.130195v2.full

I suppose you could compare AIC with and without HDOP as long as the two priors were comparable. You can also see if your autocorrelation timescales increase (they decrease with unaccounted-for location error).

Large home-range CIs either mean that the individual isn't range resident or that the duration of tracking data is very short.

Statistical efficiency of home-range estimation versus effective sample size is discussed here: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13270

When you have a nesting area and foraging area very far apart like that, that violates the stationary assumption of the base models. You would want to segment the data, estimate separate ranges, and then combine them with mean() or pkde() depending on what the areas correspond to.

I haven't explicitly coded support for sf & terra objects (I will have to at some point), but for rsf.fit() you need your rasters in a named list, like R=list(VarName=MyRaster).

Categorical variables can be whatever numbers you want, but you also have to run raster::as.factor() or they will not be detected as categorical variables.

You can put as many raster variables as you want into the R-list argument.

It doesn't look like you need an error model with that dataset. As long as your other datasets also don't have some small time intervals in them, you should be okay without it, if you need to save on computation time. It isn't hurting anything, though.

Diffusion rate is a measure of variance from an initial location over time, and will be explained in an upcoming manuscript. But it is an alternative metric for movement activity, when you don't have data that are good enough for speed/distance estimation.

Best,
Chris

I am trying to analyse site fidelity over months using the overlap() function - as I understand it, you cannot specify a certain area of the UD to calculate overlap (e.g 50% core area usage), it will only calculate overlap for the whole distribution? I thought I would be able to go down the root of exporting 50% as a shapefile/raster and then importing this again and putting it through the overlap() function but I am having trouble importing these files into the right format to be used in overlap() (e.g ctmm::UD object).

Is it even possible to do this?

Thanks,
Adam

On Tuesday, 14 February 2023 at 17:05:17 UTC chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Adam,
>
> Diffusion rate is measured in square meters of random displacement from an initial point over some amount of time.
>
> This estimate is now provided in the summary of the model fit, and that code is no longer needed.
>

> Chris

> > Would this code from a previous post still be relevant in extracting the diffusion rates?
> >
> > # FIT must be BM or IOU: CTMM=ctmm(range=FALSE) in ctmm.guess
> > diffusion <- function(FIT,level=0.95,units=TRUE)
> > {
> >   FIT$range <- TRUE
> >   DIFF <- ctmm:::area.covm(FIT$sigma)
> >   DOF <- 2*ctmm:::DOF.area(FIT)
> >   DIFF <- ctmm:::chisq.ci <http://chisq.ci/>(DIFF,DOF=DOF,level=level)
> >   if(units) { DIFF <- "km^2" %#% DIFF %#% "day" } # otherwise SI units of m^2/s
> >   return(DIFF)
> > }
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Adam

> > > Hi Adam,

> > > robust=TRUE will not help when there is no signature of velocity autocorrelation in the data, but only when the sampling distribution is heavy tailed, and velocity autocorrelation cannot be detected in part of the sampling distribution.
> > >
> > > If in your better 15-minute data, tau[velocity] is well under 3 hours (8 times per day), then there's nothing you can really do. But if you are on the margin, then you can make sure you are using all of your data as best you can - not discarding high HDOP locations and using a good location-error model.
> > >
> > > Alternative to speed estimation, you can also estimate diffusion rates if you can resolve a position autocorrelation parameter (tau[position]).
> > >
> > > Best,
> > > Chris

When I use the workflow mentioned in " Scale-insensitive estimation of speed and distance travelled from animal tracking data" I end up with a lot of Inf and 0's. As I understand, this is because my data is quite coarse (only 8 locations a day) and most of the daily models being fitted are IID. I included robust = TRUE, and all this did was change the values that were previously calculated but still left me with just as many Inf and 0's. Just wondering if there is much I can do about this because at the moment all I am able to do is get a very coarse estimate using the straight-line distances every 2 hours..

> > > > Adam

messages.body_plain:
Hi Adam,

overlap() uses the entire distribution to account for non-uniform space use. You don't want to just compare specific coverage areas. That metric assumes uniform space use within the coverage area, which is not as realistic. It's also not supported within the package, and you would have to export and do the calculation directly on the polygons.

Best,
Chris

> Hi Johanne,
>
> If Z[red]² increased, then the goodness-of-fit became worse. But I'm confused about what you are doing. Error model fitting and selection is for calibration data (not tracking data), and supplying a prior is for when you don't have calibration data.
>
> Informative prior parameters should give credible intervals that approximate the unknown prediction intervals of the population. So, in this case, GPS devices usually have a location error that ranges from a few meters to 10-20 meters at HDOP=1, and your credible intervals should reflect that. There are a number of GPS devices tested in https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.06.12.130195v2.full
>
> I suppose you could compare AIC with and without HDOP as long as the two priors were comparable. You can also see if your autocorrelation timescales increase (they decrease with unaccounted-for location error).
>
> Large home-range CIs either mean that the individual isn't range resident or that the duration of tracking data is very short.
>
> Statistical efficiency of home-range estimation versus effective sample size is discussed here: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13270
>
> When you have a nesting area and foraging area very far apart like that, that violates the stationary assumption of the base models. You would want to segment the data, estimate separate ranges, and then combine them with mean() or pkde() depending on what the areas correspond to.
>
> I haven't explicitly coded support for sf & terra objects (I will have to at some point), but for rsf.fit() you need your rasters in a named list, like R=list(VarName=MyRaster).
>
> Categorical variables can be whatever numbers you want, but you also have to run raster::as.factor() or they will not be detected as categorical variables.
>
> You can put as many raster variables as you want into the R-list argument.
>
> It doesn't look like you need an error model with that dataset. As long as your other datasets also don't have some small time intervals in them, you should be okay without it, if you need to save on computation time. It isn't hurting anything, though.
>
> Diffusion rate is a measure of variance from an initial location over time, and will be explained in an upcoming manuscript. But it is an alternative metric for movement activity, when you don't have data that are good enough for speed/distance estimation.
>
> Best,
> Chris

messages.subject: Mark-recapture data and irregular time intervals
messages.subject_clean: Mark-recapture data and irregular time intervals
messages.body_plain:
Dear Chris,

We are working on a small lizard species for which little knowledge on spatial ecology is available. The very small size of the species did not allow a telemetry monitoring. The location data collected are from a four-year mark-recapture study. We aim to estimate home ranges for 10 individuals with a number of  GPS locations ≥ 15 (mean=18.9; median=16; min=15, max=33). Monitoring sessions were conducted only in spring, between late April and mid-June. The time intervals between recaptures are very irregular. Here are the variograms for the 10 individuals, ID26 having the most GPS points and being the only one to have been recaptured during the four years. To account for the irregular data, we applied Fast=F.

We know that variograms must be stable for a reliable estimation of home ranges. Can you confirm that our variograms are unstable? We would like to know if it is still possible to estimate home ranges, despite the non-stationary behavior and the small data set? Knowing that for most individuals, the number of points collected within a year is not sufficient to segment years.

Any assistance you can provide would be greatly appreciated. The ctmm R user group is very helpful, thank you very much !

Kind regards,

Cindy

messages.body_plain:
Hi Johanne,

You need to have all UDs to be compared in one named list, like

LIST <- list(individual= Udlist[[1]][[2]],population=Udlist[[2]][[2]])
overlap(LIST)

But the grids still need to be compatible, which you can get either by calling all individuals in the same akde() call, or by using the same projection, resolution, and align.to.origin=TRUE in the grid argument.

https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/overlap.html
https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/akde.html

Best,
Chris

> >
> > Informative prior parameters should give credible intervals that approximate the unknown prediction intervals of the population. So, in this case, GPS devices usually have a location error that ranges from a few meters to 10-20 meters at HDOP=1, and your credible intervals should reflect that. There are a number of GPS devices tested in https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.06.12.130195v2.full
> >
> > I suppose you could compare AIC with and without HDOP as long as the two priors were comparable. You can also see if your autocorrelation timescales increase (they decrease with unaccounted-for location error).
> >
> > Large home-range CIs either mean that the individual isn't range resident or that the duration of tracking data is very short.
> >
> > Statistical efficiency of home-range estimation versus effective sample size is discussed here: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13270
> >
> > When you have a nesting area and foraging area very far apart like that, that violates the stationary assumption of the base models. You would want to segment the data, estimate separate ranges, and then combine them with mean() or pkde() depending on what the areas correspond to.
> >
> > I haven't explicitly coded support for sf & terra objects (I will have to at some point), but for rsf.fit() you need your rasters in a named list, like R=list(VarName=MyRaster).
> >
> > Categorical variables can be whatever numbers you want, but you also have to run raster::as.factor() or they will not be detected as categorical variables.
> >
> > You can put as many raster variables as you want into the R-list argument.
> >
> > It doesn't look like you need an error model with that dataset. As long as your other datasets also don't have some small time intervals in them, you should be okay without it, if you need to save on computation time. It isn't hurting anything, though.
> >
> > Diffusion rate is a measure of variance from an initial location over time, and will be explained in an upcoming manuscript. But it is an alternative metric for movement activity, when you don't have data that are good enough for speed/distance estimation.

> > Best,
> > Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom,

If you can put all the rasters into the same gridding (which can't be coarse compared to the home-range scale), then you should just be able to add integrator="Riemann". Then you don't have to worry about the numerical error argument and the computation time is much lower on stationary RSFs.

Otherwise, you could report the relative numerical error threshold of 5%. The default value of 1% would take 25 times longer to run than 5%. So that might also still be an option as something to leave running for a while.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: [ctmm-user] Re: Response curves and interaction among covariates in rsf.fit()
messages.subject_clean: [ctmm-user] Re: Response curves and interaction among covariates in rsf.fit()
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lorenzo,

Something like this should work:

# DATA is a telemetry object
# TREE is a raster object for tree cover
# create a boolean for day/night
DATA <- annotate(DATA)
DATA$day <- DATA$sunlight>0
DATA$night<- DATA$sunlight<=0

This would be the obvious interaction term

RSF <- rsf.fit(DATA,UD,R=list(tree=TREE),formula=~tree + tree:day)

But this model would be more interpretable:

RSF <- rsf.fit(DATA,UD,R=list(tree=TREE),formula=~tree:night + tree:day)

A difference with regular formula construction is that you want to avoid '*' because "tree*day" would expand into "tree + day + tree:day", and a 'day' term makes absolutely no sense for a spatial process model.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

This question may be trivial, but I couldn't figure out the answer myself. I am new to ctmm, and I'm trying to calculate distances travelled by birds, and I'd like to do that using the speed function. I have ca. 30 days of data for each individual, from 8AM to 7PM hourly.

My example code is as follows:

Animal <- as.telemetry(bird) # CRS 4326

GUESS_Auto <- ctmm.guess(Animal, interactive = FALSE)
fitted.mods <- ctmm.select(Animal,CTMM=GUESS_Auto,IC = "AICc",trace=3,verbose=TRUE,cores=-1)

best_model <- fitted.mods[1]

speedrk <- speed(Animal, best_model, cores =-1, robust = TRUE, fast=FALSE)

Problem is that the calculated speed is 0 (with CI: 0, Inf, Inf), and I get a warning that says "Movement model is fractal".
The results stay the same regardless of the model I choose, and calculating akde always works.

Thank you for any insight you can give me! I can also share the data if needed.

Best,
Benedetta

messages.subject: Re: speed = 0, warning "Movement model is fractal"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Benedetta,

Generally, either your data are too coarse to estimate speed/distance, or you need to include a location error model: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/error.html
Biologically, consider do your birds travel in a straight-ish line for one hour at a time?

If your data are too coarse to estimate speed/distance, then you can consider the diffusion rate estimate produced by the summary() of the fit object, as an alternative measure of movement rate.

Best,
Chris
